issues.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to the dismissal of a writ petition does not warrant condonation when the court finds no merit in condoning the delay.
material_facts: A special leave petition challenged the dismissal of a writ petition made several years earlier.
The petitioners sought condonation of the delay in challenging that dismissal.
The Court found no merit in condoning the delay.
issues.conclusion: The delay in the challenge to the first writ petition’s dismissal was not condoned.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that there was absolutely no merit for condonation of the delay. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this ruling.

predicates.special_leave_petition_challenges_writ_o: The petitioners filed a special leave petition challenging an order dismissing a writ petition.
predicates.delay_condonation_sought: The petitioners asked the court to condone delay in bringing the challenge.
predicates.challenge_was_delayed: The challenge to the writ order was brought after a period of delay.

issues.definition: When a delayed special leave petition challenges a writ order and condonation is sought, the rule states that condonation is denied.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquired for a public purpose and vested in the acquiring body after possession and payment of compensation need not be returned to its former owners merely because it is surplus or remains unused for the original purpose.
material_facts: Land was notified for acquisition under Section 126(4) of the Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act after approval of a scheme by the State Government.

Possession was taken and the Land Acquisition Officer later made an award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; the Court stated that the land vested in the Municipality free from encumbrances.
The land was used for the stated purpose, and the remaining surplus was proposed for allotment to municipal councillors and employees.
A State Government resolution provided that surplus land should first be used for another public purpose and, alternatively, returned to the former owners.
The Court stated that adequate compensation had been paid according to the market value at the time of notification.
The petitioners sought restitution of the land, and the Court declined to direct its return.
issues.conclusion: The former owners were not entitled to restitution of the acquired land; it could be used for another public purpose, and the Court would not direct its return merely because it was surplus or unused for the original purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that land acquired for a public purpose may be used for another public purpose and that land remaining unused need not be restituted to its former owner when adequate compensation has been paid. The acquisition notification was issued under Section 126(4) of the Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, and the award was made under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court cited no earlier cases.

rule.if: writ_seeks_restitution_of_acquired_land and land_acquired_for_public_purpose and possession_taken_and_land_vested and adequate_compensation_paid

predicates.writ_seeks_restitution_of_acquired_land: The claimant asks in a writ proceeding for acquired land to be returned to its former owner.
predicates.land_acquired_for_public_purpose: The land was acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.possession_taken_and_land_vested: The acquiring body took possession of the land, which then vested in that body free from encumbrances.
predicates.adequate_compensation_paid: The former owner received adequate compensation for the acquired land.

issues.definition: When a writ seeks return of land acquired for a public purpose after possession and vesting, and adequate compensation was paid, the rule denies restitution based merely on surplus land or non-use for the original purpose.
